label: Reconstruction
pitch:
The Civil War answered one question with three-quarters of a million graves: the United States would be free, not slave. It left a harder one wide open. Four million people had just been freed into a devastated South. What would their freedom actually mean? Reconstruction is the twelve-year fight over that question — the most radical, and the most violently overturned, experiment in multiracial democracy the country has ever attempted.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Three constitutional amendments in five years abolished slavery, made everyone born in the country a citizen with equal protection, and barred denying the vote by race — the biggest rewrite of the Constitution since the Bill of Rights
• Around 2,000 Black men held public office during Reconstruction, including 16 in Congress and two U.S. senators from Mississippi, the state with the largest enslaved population in 1860
• Formerly enslaved people built thousands of their own schools and churches, and founded the colleges — Howard, Fisk, Hampton, Morehouse — that still anchor Black education
• A sustained terrorist insurgency — the Ku Klux Klan, the White League, the Red Shirts — murdered its way through the Reconstruction South while the federal will to stop it slowly drained away

🤔 Why It Matters: The Fourteenth Amendment's equal-protection clause is the constitutional engine of nearly every modern civil-rights ruling. Reconstruction is where the idea that the federal government guarantees the rights of citizens against the states was born. Its overthrow set the terms of American race relations for a century, and its unfinished business is still unfinished.

🎲 Wild Card: For roughly fifty years, American schoolchildren were taught that Reconstruction failed because Black voters and 'carpetbaggers' were corrupt and incompetent and the white South nobly redeemed itself. That story — the Dunning School — was itself the propaganda victory of the people who overthrew Reconstruction by terror. The historian W. E. B. Du Bois demolished it in 1935; the textbooks took another thirty years to catch up.

details.label: Background
details.text: Even before the Civil War ended, the question of how to readmit conquered Confederate states and what to do for freed people was urgent. Lincoln issued his Ten Percent Plan in 1863; Congress countered with the harsher Wade–Davis Bill, which Lincoln pocket-vetoed.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Sherman's Special Field Order 15 set aside coastal land for freed families. Congress created the Freedmen's Bureau in March 1865. Lincoln, in his last speech, endorsed limited Black suffrage; he was assassinated five days after Appomattox.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The war settled that slavery was dead but left every question about citizenship, land, and political power unanswered, and handed them to a successor, Andrew Johnson, with neither the will nor the skill to resolve them.

details.label: Background
details.text: Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Unionist Democrat, controlled Reconstruction while Congress was out of session through late 1865. He believed restoration should be quick, lenient, and run by white Southerners.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Johnson restored ex-Confederates with pardons and returned confiscated land. Southern legislatures passed Black Codes that re-imposed near-slavery. Congress refused to seat the Confederates the South elected and broke with Johnson over the Civil Rights Act and Freedmen's Bureau veto overrides.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Johnson's policy produced a South that looked like the antebellum South with the word 'slave' removed, which radicalized Northern opinion and shifted control of Reconstruction to Congress.

details.label: Background
details.text: After the 1866 midterms gave Republicans veto-proof majorities, Congress seized control. The Reconstruction Acts of 1867 placed the South under military rule and required Black male suffrage and ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment for readmission.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: New biracial state governments wrote democratic constitutions. The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments were ratified, Johnson was impeached and acquitted by one vote, Grant was elected, and the Enforcement Acts and 1871 Klan trials briefly crushed the Klan.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: This was the high tide: Black men voted and governed across the South, public schools were created, and the Constitution was rewritten. It rested on continued Northern willingness to enforce it with troops.

details.label: Background
details.text: President Grant inherited a South in which the Klan was waging open insurgency against Black voters and Republican officials, especially around elections.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: The Enforcement Acts and the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 federalized the protection of voting and let Grant suspend habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties. Federal prosecutions broke the first Klan. The Colfax Massacre of 1873 then showed how fragile the protection was.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Federal force worked when it was applied, which is the central counterfactual of Reconstruction: its collapse was a political choice to stop applying it, not an inevitability.

details.label: Background
details.text: The Panic of 1873 turned Northern attention to the economy. Scandals discredited the Grant administration, and a wing of the Republican Party openly tired of the 'Southern question.'

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Paramilitary groups — the White League, the Red Shirts, rifle clubs — overthrew Republican governments state by state. The Mississippi Plan of 1875 perfected the method. The Supreme Court gutted federal enforcement in Cruikshank and Reese.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Reconstruction was not so much abandoned as defeated by a sustained campaign of terrorism the federal government chose to stop resisting.

spans.label: The Compromise of 1877 and the Long Afterlife

details.label: Background
details.text: The 1876 presidential election between Hayes and Tilden was disputed in three Southern states, threatening a constitutional crisis with no agreed mechanism to resolve it.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: An informal bargain awarded the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes in exchange for the withdrawal of the last federal troops protecting Republican Southern governments, which immediately collapsed.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The constitutional guarantees stayed on the page while their enforcement was withdrawn. The Lost Cause myth and the Dunning School then rewrote the history, a verdict overturned only generations later by Du Bois and Foner.

events.label: Emancipation Proclamation takes effect
events.description: On January 1, 1863, Lincoln's proclamation declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory free and authorized Black enlistment. As a war measure resting on the president's war powers, it freed no one in the loyal border states and could plausibly be unwound by a future court or peace settlement, which is exactly why a constitutional amendment would later be needed.

events.label: Lincoln's Ten Percent Plan
events.description: Lincoln's Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction offered to readmit a Confederate state once ten percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty and accepted emancipation. It was designed to shorten the war by making surrender attractive, and it set off the first fight over who controlled Reconstruction, the president or Congress.

events.label: Wade–Davis Bill pocket-vetoed
events.description: Congress passed the Wade–Davis Bill demanding that a majority of a state's white men swear loyalty before readmission, a far harsher standard than Lincoln's ten percent. Lincoln killed it with a pocket veto, and its sponsors issued the furious Wade–Davis Manifesto, the opening shot of the congressional-presidential struggle over Reconstruction.

events.label: Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15
events.description: On January 16, 1865, General Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15, setting aside a strip of confiscated coastal land from South Carolina to Florida for freed families in plots no larger than 40 acres (16 ha) — the origin of the phrase 'forty acres and a mule.' Within months, President Johnson reversed it and returned the land to its former Confederate owners.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The order came directly out of a meeting Sherman and Secretary of War Stanton held with twenty Black ministers in Savannah — the ministers' testimony about what freedpeople needed shaped the order's terms. At its peak, roughly 18,000 families were settled on about 400,000 acres before the reversal. The order also gave freed families the right to govern themselves on the reserved land with minimal military interference, making it one of the most expansive grants of Black autonomy the federal government ever issued — however briefly.

events.label: Freedmen's Bureau established
events.description: Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands in March 1865 — before the war even ended — and tasked it with feeding, housing, and managing the legal and labor affairs of four million freedpeople across the entire former Confederacy, with a one-year mandate and almost no money.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At its peak the Bureau had only about 900 agents covering the entire South — eleven states, hundreds of counties, four million people. Its full official name, 'Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands,' signaled that it also served destitute white Southerners, not only Black freedpeople. Congress debated giving it land-distribution powers from the start but declined, a decision that shaped everything that followed.

events.label: 13th Amendment passes the House
events.description: After failing once, the Thirteenth Amendment cleared the House on January 31, 1865, the legislative fight dramatized in the film Lincoln. Lincoln spent enormous political capital on it because he understood the Emancipation Proclamation was a war measure that a court or peace could unravel.

events.label: Lee surrenders at Appomattox
events.description: On April 9, 1865, Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, effectively ending the Civil War. Grant's terms were deliberately generous: Confederate soldiers were paroled and sent home rather than imprisoned for treason.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The "battle" of Appomattox Court House was actually fought on the morning of the surrender itself, when Lee made a last attempt to break through Union lines and escape, only to discover Grant's cavalry had sealed every exit. Lee had roughly 28,000 men against Grant's army of nearly 125,000. One clause in Grant's terms allowed Confederate officers to keep their sidearms and horses — a small dignity Grant insisted on to reduce the humiliation of surrender.

events.label: Lincoln's last speech endorses Black suffrage
events.description: On April 11, 1865, Lincoln gave his final public speech from a White House window, endorsing voting rights for some Black men — especially veterans and the literate — the first time any sitting American president had publicly backed Black suffrage. John Wilkes Booth was reportedly in the crowd.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The speech was primarily about Louisiana's contested new state government, which Lincoln was urging the North to accept despite its imperfections as a pragmatic step toward reunion. The endorsement of limited Black suffrage was a footnote to that argument, not its headline — which is partly why it hit Booth so hard, as even a cautious step toward Black political rights was intolerable. Lincoln's position was explicitly incremental: he was not calling for universal suffrage but arguing the question should be left to the states, threading a political needle he never got to finish threading.

events.label: Lincoln assassinated
events.description: On the night of April 14, 1865, actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C.; Lincoln died the next morning. It was the first assassination of an American president, five days after the Civil War effectively ended.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Booth's attack was part of a coordinated three-man plot the same night: a second conspirator severely stabbed Secretary of State William Seward in his sickbed, and a third lost his nerve and never attacked Vice President Andrew Johnson. Lincoln was watching the comedy "Our American Cousin" when Booth fired, having chosen a seat in the presidential box with only a single plainclothes guard, who had stepped away. Booth broke his left leg jumping from the box to the stage after firing, then escaped on horseback — yet wasn't caught for twelve days.

events.label: Andrew Johnson becomes president
events.description: Andrew Johnson, a self-educated Tennessee Democrat placed on Lincoln's 1864 ticket as a gesture of national unity, was sworn in as the 17th president on the morning of April 15, 1865. He had owned enslaved people himself and believed the United States was a white man's country — a worldview that would run unchecked for eight months before Congress reconvened.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Johnson is often remembered for being nearly drunk at his vice presidential inauguration in March 1865 — he had been ill and drank to steady himself, then delivered a rambling speech that mortified Lincoln and the Republican leadership standing nearby. He was a genuinely self-made man in a harsh sense: raised in poverty in North Carolina, he was apprenticed to a tailor as a boy, never attended school, and was taught to read largely by his wife Eliza. Yet in the Senate he was the only Southern senator from a seceding state to keep his seat and refuse to join the Confederacy.

events.label: Lincoln conspirators hanged
events.description: A military tribunal convicted eight conspirators in Booth's assassination plot; four were hanged on July 7, 1865, including Mary Surratt, the first woman executed by the federal government. The decision to try civilians before military officers rather than a civilian jury immediately became a constitutional flashpoint.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mary Surratt owned the boarding house where the plot was hatched, and her son John — also a conspirator — fled to Canada and then Europe, evading capture for over a year, meaning she was tried partly on her proximity to the plotters rather than direct action. All four defendants were hanged together in the same yard of the Old Arsenal Penitentiary, less than three months after Lincoln was shot. The other four conspirators, including the man who attacked Seward, were sentenced to life at the brutal Fort Jefferson prison in the Florida Keys.

events.label: Juneteenth: emancipation reaches Texas
events.description: On June 19, 1865, Union General Gordon Granger arrived at Galveston and announced that the enslaved people of Texas were free, more than two years after the Emancipation Proclamation, because no Union army had been there to enforce it. 'Juneteenth' became the most widely celebrated emancipation anniversary and a federal holiday in 2021.

events.label: Johnson's amnesty proclamation
events.description: In May 1865 Johnson issued a sweeping amnesty offering full pardon and property restoration to most ex-Confederates who swore a loyalty oath, while requiring the wealthiest planters and high Confederate officials to apply to him personally. He then granted those personal pardons by the thousands, handing the old ruling class back its land and political rights within months.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The $20,000 property threshold Johnson used to define who had to beg personally was enormous for the era — roughly equivalent to over half a million dollars today — and was designed to single out the planter elite. But the spectacle of proud Southern aristocrats coming to grovel before a man they'd always scorned seems to have flattered Johnson into magnanimity: by some accounts he issued hundreds of pardons in a single day. He ultimately pardoned well over 13,000 individuals under the personal-application exception, including most ex-Confederate generals and cabinet members.

events.label: Johnson installs Southern governments
events.description: Through the summer of 1865 Johnson appointed provisional governors and dictated terms for Southern states to rejoin the Union — ratify the 13th Amendment, void secession, repudiate Confederate debt — with no requirement for Black voting rights and no bar on former Confederates holding office. The restored states promptly sent ex-Confederates, including the former Confederate vice president, to Congress.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Johnson's terms required the Southern states to do almost nothing for the four million freedpeople — abolishing slavery was the bar, and it was the lowest bar imaginable. Congress, when it finally returned in December 1865, refused to seat the delegations the Southern states had elected, including Georgia's choice of Alexander Stephens as senator. That act of refusal — Congress simply declining to recognize Johnson's restored governments as legitimate — was the opening shot of the constitutional war between the branches that defined the next three years.

events.label: Black Codes enacted
events.description: Starting in fall 1865, Southern legislatures passed sweeping laws — called Black Codes — restricting freedpeople's movement, labor, land ownership, and ability to testify in court, and using vagrancy and apprenticeship laws to force them back onto plantations under conditions barely distinguishable from slavery. Mississippi and South Carolina led the way; most ex-Confederate states followed within months.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mississippi's code prohibited Black people from renting land in cities, required annual labor contracts signed before January 1 (so anyone unemployed on New Year's Day was legally a vagrant subject to forced labor), and barred Black testimony against whites in court. South Carolina's code created separate "master" and "servant" categories in law and required Black workers to get a license to work in any trade other than farming. Northern newspapers reprinted the codes in full, and the reaction was fury — the sense that the South had lost the war and was immediately reassembling the system it had fought to protect.

events.label: 13th Amendment ratified
events.description: Ratified on December 6, 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude everywhere in the United States — the first constitutional amendment in sixty years and the final, irrevocable legal answer to the question the Civil War had answered with armies.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ratification required 27 of 36 states, and Congress controversially counted the votes of several reconstructed Southern states to reach the threshold — a procedural irony, since those states' legal status was simultaneously in dispute. The amendment passed the House only on its second try: it cleared the Senate in April 1864 but initially failed in the House in June 1864 before being resubmitted and passing in January 1865, with Lincoln actively lobbying for votes (the subject of Spielberg's 2012 film).

events.label: Ku Klux Klan founded
events.description: In late 1865 or early 1866, a handful of bored Confederate veterans in Pulaski, Tennessee, started what they called a social club, took the Greek word for 'circle' (kuklos), mangled it into 'Ku Klux,' added 'Klan' for the alliteration, and within two years had built the most consequential domestic terrorist organization in American history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Historians classify the Klan as one of the earliest terrorist organizations in the United States — not a retroactive label but the contemporary understanding of its organized, political use of violence. The name's deliberate strangeness was part of the design: the nonsensical titles and outlandish costumes were meant to disorient targets and make the organization seem supernatural or unkillable. The Klan would go on to re-emerge in two more waves, in the 1910s–1920s (when it reached into Northern states and claimed millions of members) and again in the 1950s–60s as a response to the Civil Rights Movement.

events.label: Convict leasing exploits the 13th's loophole
events.description: The Thirteenth Amendment banned slavery 'except as a punishment for crime,' and Southern states immediately weaponized that clause: arrest a Black man for 'vagrancy,' convict him, and you could now constitutionally lease his labor to a planter or mine. Convict leasing was widespread by the late 1860s and persisted well into the twentieth century under conditions contemporaries described as often deadlier than chattel slavery.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Unlike enslaved workers, leased convicts represented no capital investment for the lessee — if a man died from overwork or brutality, the operator simply requested a replacement from the state. A 2008 study of Alabama convict lease records found mortality rates in some years exceeding 40 percent. The system was finally abolished at the state level in Alabama in 1928, and vestiges of forced prison labor remain constitutionally permitted today under the exception clause, a fact that drives ongoing amendment campaigns.

events.label: Freedpeople's conventions organize
events.description: Across 1865 and 1866 freedpeople held statewide conventions in Virginia, South Carolina, Tennessee, and elsewhere, demanding the vote, equal legal standing, education, and land in formal petitions to Congress. These conventions were the first organized Black political voice in the South and the seedbed of Reconstruction's Black leadership.

events.label: Memphis massacre
events.description: In May 1866 white mobs — including Memphis police and firemen — attacked the Black neighborhood of South Memphis for three days after a street confrontation involving recently discharged Black Union soldiers. Congressional investigators counted roughly 46 Black residents killed, at least five Black women raped, and 90 homes, 12 schools, and 4 churches burned.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The riot began on May 1 when white police tried to arrest Black veterans who had been mustered out of the Union Army and settled in South Memphis. What's striking is the institutional involvement: it was not a random mob but an organized assault in which city police led the violence, a fact the congressional investigating committee documented in sworn testimony. The published report, with its graphic firsthand accounts, was widely reprinted in Northern newspapers and became one of the most powerful arguments against Johnson's claim that the white South could manage Reconstruction on its own.

events.label: Civil Rights Act of 1866
events.description: The first federal law to define American citizenship, it declared every person born in the United States a citizen with equal rights to make contracts, sue, own property, and receive equal protection — a direct legal sledgehammer against the Southern Black Codes. Johnson vetoed it anyway; Congress overrode him, the first override of a major law in U.S. history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The act specifically carved out "Indians not taxed" — meaning Native people living under tribal governance — who would not receive birthright citizenship until 1924. The Radical Republicans feared the act's constitutional footing was shaky (Congress passing it under the 13th Amendment), which is exactly why they turned its guarantees into the 14th Amendment months later, making the citizenship rights harder to repeal with a simple congressional majority.

events.label: Freedmen's Bureau renewed over veto
events.description: Johnson vetoed the bill extending the Freedmen's Bureau (the federal agency managing formerly enslaved people's transition to freedom), calling it unconstitutional overreach. Congress overrode him in July 1866 — only the second veto it crushed that year — but the agency limped on underfunded until most operations shut down by 1869.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Bureau had been created in 1865 as a one-year temporary agency, so extension was simply keeping it alive. Johnson's veto message argued that Congress had no authority to create a bureau for one race, an argument Congress dismissed as a cover for abandoning freedpeople to the Black Codes. By the time the Bureau was fully wound down in 1872, it had formally supervised the signing of over a million labor contracts and established or assisted more than 1,000 schools.

events.label: 14th Amendment proposed by Congress
events.description: In June 1866 Congress passed the Fourteenth Amendment and sent it to the states: its first section made everyone born in the country a citizen, overturned the Dred Scott ruling, and for the first time required states — not just the federal government — to guarantee due process and equal protection. Southern states were told that ratification was the price of readmission to Congress.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The amendment had five sections, and the debate over each was fierce. Radicals like Thaddeus Stevens wanted immediate Black male suffrage written directly into Section 1; moderates refused, and Section 2 instead merely penalized disenfranchisement by reducing a state's congressional representation — a penalty no state ever actually paid. The Equal Protection Clause's language ('any person within its jurisdiction') was deliberately broader than 'citizen,' meaning it also protected non-citizens, a reach that still shapes immigration law today.

events.label: New Orleans massacre
events.description: On July 30, 1866, white mobs and Confederate-veteran police stormed the Mechanics' Institute in New Orleans as Louisiana Republicans tried to reconvene a state constitutional convention to give Black men the vote. The official report counted 38 dead and 146 wounded, nearly all Black; unofficial estimates ran as high as 200 killed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Many of the attackers were ex-Confederate soldiers who had recently joined the New Orleans police force — meaning the men the Union had defeated were now the city's law enforcement. Witnesses testified that Black men and white Republican delegates were shot as they raised their hands in surrender or tried to flee through windows. Because the police controlled the scene, Republican and Democratic congressional investigators returned different body counts, making the exact death toll contested to this day; what was not contested was who did the killing.

events.label: Johnson's 'Swing Around the Circle'
events.description: In the summer and fall of 1866, Johnson made an unprecedented personal speaking tour of the North — from Washington to New York, west to Chicago, south to St. Louis, and back — to campaign against the 14th Amendment and for his preferred midterm candidates. He traded insults with hecklers from the platform, compared his sufferings to Christ's, and was widely judged to have degraded the dignity of the presidency itself.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tour ran August 27 to September 15, 1866, and its nickname came from the circular route. At stop after stop, Johnson responded to heckling crowds with personal insults and ranting that shocked even some of his allies. Newspapers that had been friendly turned against him; the tour became a case study in how a president could actively destroy his own political standing. The Republican sweep in November was in part a direct verdict on what voters had watched him do on that stage.

events.label: Republican landslide in 1866 midterms
events.description: The November 1866 elections delivered Republicans more than two-thirds of both houses of Congress, a veto-proof supermajority that made Andrew Johnson a spectator on Reconstruction. Voters had seen the Memphis and New Orleans massacres and watched the Swing Around the Circle tour; the result was a referendum, and Johnson lost it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Because the ex-Confederate Southern states had not yet been re-admitted under Radical terms (most would be under the 1867 Reconstruction Acts), they largely sat out the election, meaning the electorate was already tilted heavily toward the North. The 40th Congress that resulted would push through the Reconstruction Acts, oversee the ratification of the 14th Amendment, and ultimately impeach Johnson — all made possible by the two-thirds cushion that let them override every veto he cast without needing a single Democratic vote.

events.label: Howard University chartered
events.description: Congress chartered Howard University in Washington, D.C., in March 1867, naming it for Freedmen's Bureau commissioner Oliver Otis Howard. It became the flagship of the historically Black colleges and universities that would train the Black professional class for the century of Jim Crow ahead.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Howard was unusual among the new Black colleges in being federally chartered and receiving federal funding from the start, which gave it more resources and stability than church-backed peers. Within its first decade it had established law, medical, and theology schools — the law school would produce Thurgood Marshall, who argued Brown v. Board of Education, a thread that runs forward through this chain. Howard was also briefly home to Frederick Douglass, who served on its board and lived nearby on his Cedar Hill estate.

events.label: Fisk University founded
events.description: Fisk University opened in Nashville in January 1866, founded by American Missionary Association teachers and Freedmen's Bureau support in a former Union Army hospital. It became one of the most academically rigorous of the new Black colleges and gave the world the Fisk Jubilee Singers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Fisk's 40-acre campus, including its landmark Jubilee Hall — paid for by the Jubilee Singers' touring proceeds — is a National Historic District. The university admitted both men and women from the start and established a college-preparatory curriculum at a time when most white Southerners believed Black people incapable of higher learning. W. E. B. Du Bois graduated from Fisk in 1888, and the experience of teaching in rural Tennessee that summer shaped his lifelong understanding of the Black South.

events.label: Reconstruction Acts of 1867
events.description: Between March 1867 and March 1868, Congress passed four Reconstruction Acts over Johnson's vetoes, declaring the existing Southern state governments illegitimate and dividing ten ex-Confederate states into five military districts commanded by U.S. Army generals — the most aggressive exercise of federal power the nineteenth century produced.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The acts were passed by Congress's automatic two-thirds Republican majority, so Johnson's vetoes were overridden the same day they were issued in some cases, a procedural speed that underscored how completely Congress had stripped the presidency of influence over Reconstruction. The acts required not just ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment but new state constitutions drafted by conventions elected by universal male suffrage — a deliberate reversal of the Black Codes that had just stripped Black men of political standing.

events.label: Five military districts established
events.description: The Reconstruction Acts placed the ten reconstructed states under five U.S. Army district commanders — including Philip Sheridan in Louisiana and Texas, and John Schofield in Virginia — who had sweeping power to remove obstructionist officials, protect voter registration, and override discriminatory local rulings. Under army supervision, roughly 700,000 Black men and 660,000 white men were enrolled as voters, a near-instant transformation of the Southern electorate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sheridan was particularly aggressive: he removed the governors of Louisiana and Texas within months of taking command, calling one of them an 'impediment to reconstruction.' Grant, his commander, had to warn him to slow down for political reasons. At its Reconstruction peak the army had about 20,000 soldiers spread across the five districts — a thin force for a region the size of Western Europe, which helps explain why armed white-supremacist groups could overwhelm it when federal will faltered.

events.label: Tenure of Office Act
events.description: Passed over Johnson's veto on March 2, 1867, the Tenure of Office Act forbade the president from removing Senate-confirmed officials without Senate approval — a law Congress designed specifically to protect Secretary of War Stanton and keep Reconstruction's enforcement machinery out of Johnson's hands.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The law remained on the books in weakened form until 1887, when Congress finally repealed it. In 1926, the Supreme Court (in Myers v. United States) ruled a similar law unconstitutional, vindicating the constitutional objection Johnson's lawyers had raised at trial. The act applied not just to cabinet officers but to any civil official confirmed by the Senate, covering a much broader range of appointments than the Stanton fight alone.

events.label: Alaska Purchase ('Seward's Folly')
events.description: Secretary of State William Seward bought Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million, about two cents an acre, mocked at the time as 'Seward's Icebox.' It signaled that even during the Reconstruction crisis the United States was thinking continentally and as an emerging power.

events.label: Union Leagues organize Black voters
events.description: The Union League, originally a genteel Northern pro-war club, was remade after 1867 into a grassroots political network across the South — meeting in Black churches and schoolhouses, often at night and armed — that taught freedmen how to register, vote, and understand the new laws.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The League's meetings were semi-secret partly to protect members from violence, with rituals and oaths borrowed from fraternal-lodge culture that freedpeople already knew. This made the League deeply threatening to planters, who saw it as a disciplined political organization rather than just a club. Local Union League leaders became among the first targets of early Klan terror precisely because they were the organizing backbone of the Black Republican vote.

events.label: Biracial constitutional conventions
events.description: In 1867 and 1868, ten Southern states held constitutional conventions under army supervision in which Black delegates participated as elected representatives for the first time — in some states constituting a majority of delegates. These conventions produced the most democratic constitutions the region had ever seen, creating public school systems, eliminating property qualifications, and guaranteeing civil rights.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: South Carolina's convention was majority Black — 76 of 124 delegates were Black men, most of them formerly enslaved. Louisiana's convention was nearly half Black. The constitutions they drafted were so broadly democratic that some survived in amended form for decades; South Carolina's 1868 constitution, for instance, remained in effect (with modifications) until 1895, when a new 'Redeemer' constitution systematically undid its provisions. The Dunning School historians would spend the next fifty years characterizing these conventions as corrupt farce — a characterization later scholarship demolished.

events.label: Hampton Institute founded
events.description: Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute opened in Virginia in 1868, founded by Freedmen's Bureau general Samuel Chapman Armstrong to train Black teachers and trades workers. Its most famous graduate, Booker T. Washington, carried its vocational model forward into the Jim Crow era.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Armstrong had commanded Black Union troops during the war and believed that industrial training, not classical education, was the right path for freedpeople — a conviction that shaped Hampton's entire curriculum and generated fierce controversy. Hampton also admitted Native American students from 1878, part of a federal policy of assimilating Indigenous youth that used the same vocational model. Washington graduated in 1875 and founded Tuskegee Institute in Alabama in 1881 on explicit Hampton principles, setting up the major debate with Du Bois over industrial vs. liberal-arts education that would define Black intellectual life for decades.

events.label: Johnson fires Secretary Stanton
events.description: In February 1868 Johnson dismissed Edwin Stanton — Lincoln's meticulous, combative secretary of war who had aligned fully with Radical Republicans — knowing full well it violated the Tenure of Office Act and would trigger impeachment. Stanton refused to leave his War Department office, barricading himself inside for weeks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Stanton had first been appointed attorney general under James Buchanan, then moved to the War Department under Lincoln in 1862, where he became one of the most powerful cabinet officers of the entire war. He ran the department with an obsessive grip on logistics that infuriated generals but helped keep Union armies supplied. After Johnson's acquittal, Stanton resigned; he died just four days after being confirmed to the Supreme Court in December 1869, never having served a single day on the bench.

events.label: Andrew Johnson impeached
events.description: On February 24, 1868, the House voted 126 to 47 to impeach Andrew Johnson — the first time in American history — on eleven articles, most of them built around his firing of Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in defiance of the Tenure of Office Act. Impeachment is only an indictment, not removal; conviction still required a two-thirds Senate vote.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The House adopted the articles in two batches — the main resolution on March 2 and additional articles on March 3, 1868, the day before Congress adjourned. Lorenzo Thomas, the adjutant general Johnson named as acting secretary, tried to physically take possession of the War Department office and was briefly arrested before charges were dropped. The full trial before the Senate, with Chief Justice Salmon Chase presiding, lasted roughly two months and produced thousands of pages of testimony.

events.label: Johnson acquitted by one vote
events.description: On May 16, 1868, the Senate voted 35–19 to convict on the key article — exactly one vote short of the 36 needed — and Johnson was acquitted, surviving to finish his term as a politically broken and effectively powerless president. Grant's election later that year was already a foregone conclusion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Seven Republicans voted to acquit; the Senate then recessed for ten days before voting on two more articles, producing the same 35–19 result, after which the trial was adjourned. Johnson celebrated his acquittal but won zero political capital from it: his own party didn't nominate him and the Democrats passed over him too. The Tenure of Office Act, the law at the center of the whole crisis, was quietly stripped of its teeth just two years later, in 1869, under Grant.

events.label: 14th Amendment ratified
events.description: Ratified in July 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment made all persons born in the United States citizens and barred states from denying due process or equal protection of the law. It was designed to give Congress and the courts the tools to protect freed people — tools the Supreme Court would spend the next two decades blunting.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Three former Confederate states — Georgia, Ohio, and New Jersey — initially ratified and then tried to rescind their ratifications, raising questions Congress resolved by simply declaring ratification complete anyway. The amendment overturned the 1857 Dred Scott ruling, which had held that Black Americans could never be citizens. Its citizenship clause has since been invoked in cases ranging from women's suffrage to same-sex marriage to college admissions — making it the single most litigated provision of the entire Constitution.

events.label: Opelousas and St. Bernard massacres
events.description: In the weeks before the 1868 presidential election, white Democrats in Louisiana killed an estimated 150 or more Black people around Opelousas and St. Bernard Parish to suppress the Republican vote. Louisiana, narrowly carried by Grant statewide, recorded almost no Republican votes in the terrorized parishes.

events.label: Ulysses S. Grant elected president
events.description: The Union's winning general won the 1868 election on the slogan 'Let us have peace,' pledging to defend Reconstruction. His national popular-vote margin was narrow enough that the roughly 500,000 newly enfranchised Black voters in the reconstructed Southern states were plausibly the difference.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Grant's opponent, Horatio Seymour of New York, ran on a platform hostile to Reconstruction and had opposed the draft during the war. The 1868 contest was the first presidential election in which Black men could legally vote in the South under the First Reconstruction Act — yet several ex-Confederate states were still not readmitted and cast no electoral votes at all. Grant carried the Electoral College 214 to 80, a far wider margin than his popular-vote lead suggested.

events.label: 14th Amendment and corporate personhood
events.description: Almost immediately after the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868, corporations began arguing in court that its protection of 'persons' applied to them. By the 1880s–1930s, the amendment written to protect freed slaves was being used far more often to strike down railroad regulation and labor laws than to protect Black citizens.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The legal theory took hold through a string of cases in the 1880s in which railroads successfully argued that state regulations violated their due process rights as 'persons.' Between 1868 and 1912, the Supreme Court used the Fourteenth Amendment in 28 cases involving Black civil rights and 312 cases involving corporate rights — roughly an eleven-to-one ratio. The NAACP's litigation strategy from the 1930s onward was essentially a campaign to reclaim the amendment for the people it had been written to protect.

events.label: 15th Amendment proposed
events.description: Congress sent the Fifteenth Amendment to the states in February 1869, barring denial of the vote by race but pointedly leaving silent any mention of poll taxes, literacy tests, or property requirements. That silence was not an oversight — the radicals who wanted a positive, affirmative right to vote lost the floor fight, and the weaker negative prohibition was what passed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Senate debated but rejected language that would have guaranteed affirmative voting rights regardless of 'educational or religious tests, property, or creed' — a version that would have made poll taxes and literacy tests unconstitutional on its face. The narrower text passed because several Northern states worried that broad language might also ban their own literacy requirements, which were aimed at immigrants. It took 25 states to ratify a constitutional amendment at the time; the required threshold was met on February 3, 1870, with ratifications coming from both Northern and former Confederate states.

events.label: Women's suffrage movement splits
events.description: The Fifteenth Amendment's enfranchisement of Black men but not women fractured the women's rights movement in 1869: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony formed the National Woman Suffrage Association opposing the amendment as written, while Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe's American Woman Suffrage Association backed it. The schism, sharpened by racism in the anti-amendment wing, lasted until 1890.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The NWSA, Stanton and Anthony's organization, focused on a federal constitutional amendment and excluded men from full membership. Stone's AWSA was open to men and preferred a state-by-state approach. Stanton's public arguments against the amendment included explicit claims that educated white women were more deserving of the vote than 'ignorant' Black men — language that haunted the movement's memory for generations. The two organizations did not reunite into the National American Woman Suffrage Association until 1890.

events.label: Transcontinental Railroad completed
events.description: On May 10, 1869, a golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory, joined the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads, linking the Atlantic coast rail network to San Francisco Bay for the first time. Built across 1,911 miles (3,075 km) of plains, mountains, and desert, it remade American commerce and accelerated the collision with Native nations on the Plains.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Central Pacific workforce was roughly 80 percent Chinese immigrants, most brought over specifically for the project; the Union Pacific relied heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. The federal government financed construction through land grants totaling millions of acres alongside the right-of-way — land that was, in most cases, treaty-guaranteed Native territory. The entire line was built in six years; contemporaries called it the greatest engineering feat of the century.

events.label: Black Friday gold panic
events.description: On September 24, 1869, speculators Jay Gould and James Fisk tried to corner the entire U.S. gold market, exploiting their connection to Abel Corbin — Grant's brother-in-law — to believe the Treasury would stay out. When Treasury Secretary Boutwell finally dumped $4 million in government gold, the price collapsed in minutes and ruined hundreds of traders.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gould and Fisk had run the gold price from about $132 to nearly $163 per ounce over a few weeks before the crash. The Gold Room on New York's Exchange Place descended into near-riot as prices swung violently; several brokers reportedly suffered nervous breakdowns on the floor. Gould, forewarned that the Treasury was about to act, had quietly started selling his own gold holdings while still publicly driving the price up — leaving Fisk and smaller speculators to absorb the losses. A congressional investigation concluded Grant was not personally complicit but that his brother-in-law had actively misled him.

events.label: Hiram Revels enters the Senate
events.description: In February 1870 Hiram Rhodes Revels, a free-born African Methodist Episcopal minister and Union Army chaplain from Mississippi, became the first Black American ever to sit in Congress — taking a Senate seat that had previously belonged to Confederate president Jefferson Davis.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Revels was born free in North Carolina and had voted in Ohio before the war, which became the crux of the Senate debate over seating him: opponents argued he hadn't been a citizen for the required nine years, because the Dred Scott ruling had stripped Black citizenship until the 14th Amendment. He served only a partial unexpired term, then returned to Mississippi to become president of Alcorn University, one of the first Black land-grant colleges.

events.label: 15th Amendment ratified
events.description: Ratified in February 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment barred denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. It was the last of the three Reconstruction amendments and, for a few years, made Black men a decisive political force across the South — until the loopholes it left open were methodically exploited.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The amendment's narrow wording — forbidding only race-based denial, not the poll taxes or literacy tests that would do the same work — was not accidental: broader drafts that would have banned property and literacy qualifications outright were rejected to secure enough votes for ratification. The first Black senator and the first Black House members were elected under its protection in 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to make the amendment's promise functional in the states that had circumvented it for 95 years.

events.label: Black justice on a state supreme court
events.description: Jonathan Jasper Wright, a Pennsylvania-trained Black lawyer, was elected to the South Carolina Supreme Court in 1870 and served seven years — the first Black American to sit on any state's highest court.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wright had come south as a Freedmen's Bureau agent, one of the first Black lawyers admitted to the Pennsylvania bar, and then built a South Carolina political career. He authored several substantial opinions on constitutional and property questions during his tenure. When Redemption came in 1877, he was forced off the court through manufactured ethics charges that were widely understood as pretextual; he died in poverty in 1885.

events.label: Joseph Rainey enters the House
events.description: Joseph Rainey of South Carolina, born enslaved, became the first Black member of the U.S. House of Representatives in December 1870 and served five terms, the longest tenure of any Black congressman of the Reconstruction era.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: During the Civil War, Rainey and his wife had escaped to Bermuda after he was pressed into labor building Confederate fortifications — they returned to South Carolina only after the war ended. He was also the first Black congressman to preside over the House of Representatives, filling the Speaker's chair during chamber debates. His five terms ended when violent intimidation and ballot-stuffing by white Democrats made his district effectively unwinnable in 1879.

events.label: Robert Smalls in public office
events.description: Robert Smalls, the enslaved harbor pilot who commandeered the Confederate steamer Planter under fire of the harbor forts in May 1862 and sailed it to the Union blockade, went on to serve five terms in Congress from South Carolina and helped write the state's Reconstruction constitution.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: After delivering the Planter, Smalls personally lobbied President Lincoln to allow Black men to serve as Union soldiers — and Lincoln agreed within months, a policy shift that brought roughly 180,000 Black men into the Union Army. After Reconstruction's collapse, Smalls tried to hold his House seat for years through repeated contested elections, each one challenged by Democrats who used fraud and violence; he finally lost for good in 1886. He later bought the Beaufort, South Carolina, house where he had been born into slavery.

events.label: First Enforcement Act
events.description: The first Enforcement Act, passed in May 1870, made it a federal crime to use force or intimidation to stop citizens from voting, putting the full weight of federal courts and marshals behind the Fifteenth Amendment for the first time and transforming what had been a state policing problem into a federal one.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before the Enforcement Acts, the Fifteenth Amendment existed on paper but had no criminal enforcement mechanism — a right without a remedy. The 1870 act also protected the right of Black men to hold office and serve on juries, not just to vote, closing loopholes that had been used to hollow out formal equality. It was passed alongside the creation of the Department of Justice (also 1870), giving Congress both the law and the prosecutorial institution to enforce it simultaneously.

events.label: Second Enforcement Act
events.description: The second Enforcement Act, passed in February 1871, put federal elections in large cities under direct federal supervision, appointing election overseers and deputy marshals empowered to police polling places — extending Washington's reach into Northern urban machine politics as well as Southern terror.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: By covering large Northern cities alongside the Southern counties most ravaged by Klan violence, the act made a political point: this was a national voting-rights law, not a Southern occupation measure, which helped (for a time) to hold together the coalition needed to pass it. The federal supervisors it created had the power to make arrests at polling places, a direct answer to the pattern of intimidation at the ballot box that had been documented throughout the South.

events.label: Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871
events.description: The Ku Klux Klan Act of April 1871, the third and strongest of the Enforcement Acts, authorized the president to deploy the army against conspiracies to deny civil rights and to suspend habeas corpus (the ancient legal right requiring the government to bring any arrested person before a court) — formally classifying Klan terror as a rebellion against the United States.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Suspending habeas corpus is an extraordinary constitutional power, permitted only in cases of rebellion or invasion; Congress had last done it during the Civil War. The act went further than prior laws by making the conspiracy itself a federal crime, not just the individual act — meaning organizers, not just night-riders, could be prosecuted. It also allowed private citizens to sue Klan members in federal court for civil rights violations, a provision that would be cited more than a century later in modern civil rights litigation.

events.label: Congress investigates the Klan
events.description: In 1871–72 a joint congressional committee took sworn testimony from victims and witnesses across the South and published a thirteen-volume report documenting Klan whippings, rapes, mutilations, murders, and the burning of schools and churches — one of the fullest first-person records of organized racial terror in American history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The scale of the record was unprecedented: thousands of pages of sworn testimony, making denial structurally difficult in a way that oral accounts or newspaper reports were not. The report documented that Klan violence spiked specifically around elections — confirming the political rather than merely criminal character of the terror. As a government-compiled, sworn account of a paramilitary war on a functioning multiracial franchise, historians have noted it has few true rivals among atrocity records of the same era.

events.label: South Carolina Klan trials
events.description: In October 1871 President Grant suspended habeas corpus (the right to be charged before being jailed) in nine South Carolina counties, and federal authorities arrested and indicted hundreds of Klansmen — breaking the first Ku Klux Klan as a functioning organization within two years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 made Klan-style conspiracies a federal offense for the first time, allowing prosecutions to bypass hostile state courts. The South Carolina crackdown was the clearest proof that the federal government had the legal tools and the military capacity to defend Black citizens — making the 1875 refusal to use those same tools in Mississippi a deliberate choice, not a helpless shrug.

events.label: Amnesty Act of 1872
events.description: Passed May 22, 1872, the Amnesty Act restored political and officeholding rights to the vast majority of former Confederates who had been barred by Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment. It returned thousands of experienced white Southern Democratic politicians to the electoral arena just as Northern willingness to enforce Black voting rights was beginning to crack.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment had targeted anyone who previously swore an oath to uphold the Constitution and then supported the Confederacy — a category covering most of the antebellum South's political and military leadership. The act passed with a large bipartisan majority, with many Republicans arguing that ten years had been long enough and reconciliation required it. About 500 individuals with prominent enough records — the highest Confederate officeholders and generals — were excluded and remained barred until a separate 1898 act finally lifted all remaining penalties.

events.label: Freedman's Savings Bank
events.description: Chartered by Congress in 1865 to help formerly enslaved people build financial security, the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company attracted deposits from tens of thousands of Black customers before speculative mismanagement and outright looting drove it into insolvency; it collapsed in 1874, wiping out roughly $3 million in Black savings.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Frederick Douglass was appointed president of the bank in early 1874 in a last-ditch effort to restore confidence — and personally invested $10,000 of his own money — before realizing the institution was already beyond saving. Congress never reimbursed depositors in full; most received about 60 cents on the dollar in a drawn-out claims process, and many received nothing. The bank's failure was a profound economic blow to communities that had trusted a federal charter as a guarantee of safety, and it deepened distrust of financial institutions among Black Americans for decades.

events.label: Liberal Republican revolt
events.description: A faction of reform-minded Republicans, fed up with corruption and openly tired of Reconstruction, bolted in 1872 and ran newspaper editor Horace Greeley for president on a platform of civil service reform and 'letting the South manage its own affairs.' The Democrats endorsed Greeley too. Grant crushed them, but their revolt announced that elite Northern opinion was shifting away from Black civil rights.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Liberal Republican movement was anchored in Missouri, organized by Senator Carl Schurz, himself a German immigrant who had championed abolition — yet who was now calling Reconstruction a failed experiment. Greeley, founder of the New York Tribune, had spent his career urging abolition but had also famously signed the bail bond for Jefferson Davis after the war, a gesture of reconciliation that cost him support on both sides. Greeley was so devastated by the campaign — his wife died during it and he lost badly — that he died just 24 days after the election, before the Electoral College met.

events.label: Crédit Mobilier scandal exposed
events.description: Insiders of the Union Pacific railroad created a shell company called Crédit Mobilier, paid themselves enormous construction-contract profits, then spread discounted stock among key congressmen to buy silence — a bribery scheme exposed by the New York Sun in 1872 that touched the sitting vice president and future president James Garfield.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Crédit Mobilier was a real French construction firm whose name was borrowed to lend the scheme an air of respectability. The investigation found that the company had collected about $23 million for work that cost only $16 million — the difference went to Union Pacific insiders. Vice President Schuyler Colfax was so badly damaged that he was dropped from the 1872 ticket, replaced by Henry Wilson. The scandal is widely credited with making the word 'railroad' synonymous with political corruption for the rest of the century.

events.label: Grant re-elected
events.description: Ulysses Grant won his second term in November 1872 by a wide margin, crushing Horace Greeley in the electoral college 286 to 66. It was the last presidential election in which the Reconstruction coalition held a clear national majority, with Black voters in the South still largely able to cast ballots.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Greeley died on November 29, 1872 — three weeks after election day but before the Electoral College formally voted — making him the only major-party presidential candidate in U.S. history to die in the interval between the popular vote and the electoral vote. His 66 pledged electors scattered their votes among four other candidates rather than cast them for a dead man. Grant's margin in the popular vote was over 11 percentage points, but Northern voter turnout had already begun to decline from its 1868 peak, a quiet early signal of political exhaustion.

events.label: Pinchback acting governor of Louisiana
events.description: P. B. S. Pinchback served 35 days as acting governor of Louisiana in late 1872 and early 1873 when the sitting governor was impeached, making him the first Black governor in American history — a record that stood until 1990.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Pinchback was the son of a white Mississippi planter and an enslaved woman he had freed; he grew up partly in Cincinnati and served as a Union officer commanding a company of Black soldiers. After his governorship, Louisiana's legislature elected him to the U.S. Senate, but a hostile Senate refused to seat him after a three-year delay, citing disputed election procedures — a rejection widely understood as racial. He was also the first American of African descent to head a state's executive branch.

events.label: Slaughter-House Cases
events.description: The Supreme Court's first major Fourteenth Amendment ruling came not in a racial-justice case but a meatpacking dispute — and it quietly gutted the amendment anyway, reading the 'privileges or immunities' clause so narrowly that it protected almost nothing against state abuse.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The vote was 5-4, and the dissents were scathing: Justice Stephen Field argued the majority had made the amendment 'a vain and idle enactment.' The case was decided just five years after the amendment was ratified, meaning the Court dismantled its main protective gear almost before it was ever used. Because Slaughter-House left the Privileges or Immunities Clause nearly hollow, later courts had to build civil-rights protections awkwardly through the Due Process Clause instead — a workaround that shaped constitutional law for the next 150 years.

events.label: Colfax massacre
events.description: On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, a white mob — including former Confederate soldiers and Klan members — attacked Black militiamen defending the parish courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana, following a disputed election. Between 62 and 153 Black men were killed, the majority of them after they had surrendered.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The attackers used a small cannon to overwhelm the defenders, making it an organized military assault, not a spontaneous riot. Many of the men killed after surrendering were executed by gunshot to the back of the head, and bodies were dumped in the Red River, which is why the death toll remains uncertain. It remains the single deadliest act of racial violence in the entire Reconstruction era, and the site today has a state historical marker that, for much of the 20th century, described it as a 'riot' won by 'brave' whites.

events.label: Panic of 1873
events.description: On September 18, 1873, the banking house of Jay Cooke & Company — which had financed the Union's war debt — collapsed under the weight of over-extended railroad loans, triggering a stock market shutdown and the start of the worst American economic crisis of the nineteenth century.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The panic actually started in Vienna in May 1873, where a railroad and land speculation bubble burst first, then spread westward through European banks before reaching the U.S. — making it arguably the first global financial crisis of the industrial age. The New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days after Cooke's failure, the only time it had shut down since its founding. The crash revealed that the Northern railroad boom had been massively over-capitalized: at the time of the panic, more railroad track had been laid in the U.S. in the previous decade than in all of Europe combined.

events.label: Bradwell v. Illinois
events.description: Myra Bradwell passed the Illinois bar exam and was denied a license anyway — because she was a woman. The Supreme Court upheld the state, and one justice wrote a concurring opinion explaining that God had assigned women to the domestic sphere, not the courtroom.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bradwell had founded the Chicago Legal News in 1868 and built it into one of the most widely read legal newspapers in the country — while being barred from practicing law. The concurrence by Justice Joseph Bradley, declaring the 'natural and proper timidity' of women unfit for public life, was not the majority's official reasoning but became the most quoted part of the decision. Illinois eventually admitted women to the bar by statute in 1872, before the Supreme Court ruled, but the federal constitutional question was settled against women regardless.

events.label: Coushatta massacre
events.description: In August 1874 the White League in Coushatta, Louisiana, forced six white Republican officeholders to resign, then murdered them along with five to twenty Black witnesses as the group fled under a promise of safe passage. Killing white Republicans demonstrated the counter-revolution was no longer just about suppressing Black voters — it was about eliminating Republican government entirely.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The victims included the parish sheriff, a state senator, and four other officials, all white, which removed any argument that the White League's violence was purely about racial hierarchy rather than outright political extermination. The killings happened despite an explicit pledge of safe conduct given by the League itself, meaning the violation of the promise was part of the message. No one was ever tried for the Coushatta murders.

events.label: White League organizes in Louisiana
events.description: The White League, formed openly in Louisiana in 1874, was the first major post-Klan paramilitary to ditch the hood: it drilled in uniform, declared its goal of overthrowing the Republican government by force, and recruited heavily from the Confederate veterans who had just committed the Colfax massacre.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The League's first chapter formed in Grant Parish — the exact parish where the Colfax massacre happened three months earlier — making the organizational continuity between massacre and militia explicit. Unlike the Klan, which the federal government had successfully prosecuted in 1871–72, the White League operated in the open because it had correctly read that Washington no longer had the will to pursue it. The Thomas Nast illustration on its lead image, titled 'Worse than Slavery,' ran in Harper's Weekly in 1874 and depicted the White League and KKK as twin forces crushing Black Southerners between them.

events.label: Battle of Liberty Place
events.description: On September 14, 1874, roughly 5,000 White League fighters defeated the racially integrated New Orleans Metropolitan Police and state militia in open street combat, seized the statehouse and armory, and held them for three days — an outright coup — before standing down only when President Grant ordered federal troops to the city.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At least 35 people died in the fighting, including at least 21 White League members, making it a genuine military engagement, not a mob action. Not a single insurgent was charged or prosecuted for the insurrection. The city of New Orleans later erected a monument to the White League victory at the site on Canal Street, which became a flashpoint for Confederate monument debates and was finally removed in 2017.

events.label: Democrats sweep the 1874 midterms
events.description: In November 1874, amid the ongoing economic depression (the Panic of 1873) and Republican corruption fatigue, Democrats swept the House for the first time since 1859 — gaining 93 seats. With Congress now divided, the legislative machinery that had funded and authorized Reconstruction enforcement stopped.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Republican loss of 93 House seats in a single election remains one of the largest partisan swings in American congressional history. The new Democratic majority immediately began defunding enforcement, refusing to appropriate money for federal marshals and troops in the South. The 1874 election is the precise hinge point where Reconstruction's political engine — dependent on Republican control of all three branches — lost one of its three legs and never recovered it.

events.label: Vicksburg massacre
events.description: In December 1874 armed white Democrats in Vicksburg, Mississippi, forcibly removed the Black sheriff, Peter Crosby, and then killed an estimated 150 to 300 Black residents in the city and surrounding Warren County over the following weeks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sheriff Crosby was shot in the head after being reinstated — a direct assassination of a sitting elected officer. The Vicksburg massacre killed far more people than the better-known Clinton attack the following year, yet it attracted less lasting federal response, functioning as a proof-of-concept that mass violence against Black officials would go largely unpunished.

events.label: Civil Rights Act of 1875
events.description: Pushed through Congress as a dying memorial to Senator Charles Sumner, the Civil Rights Act of 1875 was the first federal public-accommodations law: it guaranteed Black Americans equal access to inns, theaters, public transport, and jury service regardless of race. It went largely unenforced from the moment of passage and was struck down entirely by the Supreme Court in 1883.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sumner had originally drafted the bill in 1870, but it took nearly five years and his death in 1874 to get it passed — his colleagues pushed it through as a tribute. President Grant, who signed it, had actually preferred different anti-violence measures and gave the act little enforcement priority. The Supreme Court's 1883 ruling that Congress lacked authority to ban private discrimination would stand for eighty-one years, until the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

events.label: Page Act of 1875
events.description: The Page Act barred 'undesirable' immigrants, in practice mostly Chinese women presumed to be prostitutes, the first restrictive federal immigration law. It showed that the same Congress writing equality into the Constitution for freedpeople was simultaneously building racial exclusion against Asian immigrants.

events.label: Blanche Bruce enters the Senate
events.description: Blanche K. Bruce, born enslaved in Virginia, won a full Mississippi Senate seat in 1875 and served the complete six-year term, the first Black senator to do so and the first to preside over the Senate chamber. No Black American won a Senate election again until Edward Brooke in 1966.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bruce had educated himself partly by running a school for freedpeople in Missouri, then made his way to Mississippi during Reconstruction, where he built a cotton plantation and political career from almost nothing. Beyond the Senate, he was later appointed Register of the Treasury under Presidents Garfield and Harrison — meaning his signature appeared on U.S. currency — one of the highest federal positions held by a Black American in the 19th century.

events.label: Minor v. Happersett
events.description: Virginia Minor, a Missouri suffragist, tried to register to vote in 1872 and was turned away. Her case reached the Supreme Court, which ruled unanimously that citizenship and the right to vote were entirely separate things — meaning the Fourteenth Amendment gave women citizenship but not the ballot.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Minor's husband, Francis Minor, argued the case alongside her — because Missouri law did not allow married women to sue in their own names. The ruling was unanimous, with no dissent at all, which meant suffragists lost their most promising legal shortcut and were forced back to the long road of state-by-state campaigns and, eventually, a new amendment. The decision stood for 45 years until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

events.label: The Mississippi Plan
events.description: The Mississippi Plan of 1875 was a Democratic Party blueprint for overthrowing a legally elected Republican state government through coordinated economic coercion, paramilitary violence, and deniable provocation — discussed openly in the Democratic press as the intended strategy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Democrats articulated their aim bluntly: regain the legislature 'peaceably if we can, forcibly if we must.' The plan worked so well that it became the exported template — every Southern state adopted a version after 1875, and Mississippi's own 1890 disfranchisement constitution codified its logic in law.

events.label: Clinton massacre
events.description: At a Republican barbecue in Clinton, Mississippi, in September 1875, white paramilitary rifle clubs opened fire on a crowd of roughly 3,000, then hunted Black residents through the surrounding countryside for days, killing an estimated 20 to 50 people.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Among those targeted was Charles Caldwell, a Black state senator and former soldier who had helped organize the meeting; he was assassinated in December 1875, a few months after the massacre, in a coordinated act of political elimination. The Clinton attack was one of a series of rifle-club assaults that fall, all designed to collapse Black Republican turnout before election day.

events.label: Grant refuses troops to Mississippi
events.description: When Governor Ames formally requested federal troops to stop the Mississippi Plan's terror campaign in 1875, the Grant administration declined in writing — Attorney General Edwards Pierrepont conveying that 'the whole public are tired out with these annual autumnal outbreaks in the South.'

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The refusal was also driven by a concrete political calculation: sending troops would cost Republicans the pivotal state of Ohio in that fall's off-year elections. This was a documented, deliberate trade — a Black-majority state's democracy for a Northern state's electoral math — made by the same administration that had proven, just four years earlier in South Carolina, that troops actually worked.

events.label: Whiskey Ring scandal
events.description: A vast conspiracy of distillers and Treasury officials operating from 1871 to 1875 diverted millions in whiskey excise taxes into private pockets and Republican campaign funds, the ring's kingpin being Grant's own appointee as Revenue Collector of Missouri — until Treasury Secretary Benjamin Bristow broke it open.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ring defrauded the government of an estimated $3 million in tax revenue (about $80 million today). Bristow used a novel tactic to expose it: he bypassed the normal Treasury channels — which were compromised — and had trusted agents secretly gather evidence before any ring members could be warned. Grant's private secretary Orville Babcock was indicted; Grant submitted a deposition defending him and Babcock was acquitted, a moment that made the president look as if he was shielding a criminal. Over 230 people were ultimately convicted.

events.label: United States v. Cruikshank
events.description: In 1876 the Supreme Court overturned the federal Colfax convictions in United States v. Cruikshank, ruling that the Fourteenth Amendment restrained only state governments — not private individuals — meaning federal courts had no power to punish a private racial massacre, however large.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Chief Justice Morrison Waite authored the opinion, which also gutted the Second Amendment's application to states, ruling that the right to bear arms was not a right the federal government could protect against state or private infringement. The decision effectively made the Enforcement Acts of 1870–71 unenforceable as tools against private paramilitary violence, which was the only enforcement mechanism that had worked against the Klan. Cruikshank's logic remained the constitutional baseline until the 20th century civil rights era, nearly a century of judicially licensed impunity.

events.label: United States v. Reese
events.description: Two Kentucky election officials refused to count a Black man's vote and were prosecuted under the Enforcement Acts. The Supreme Court struck down the key sections of those acts, ruling that the Fifteenth Amendment did not positively grant the right to vote — it only barred a few specifically named reasons for denying it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Court's distinction sounds technical but had enormous practical consequences: because the Fifteenth Amendment only banned denial 'on account of race,' facially race-neutral barriers like poll taxes and literacy tests were left entirely untouched. The Black voter in the case, William Garner, never got to cast his ballot, and the officials who turned him away faced no penalty. Reese effectively handed states a roadmap for disfranchisement that would be followed for the next 90 years.

events.label: Hamburg massacre
events.description: In July 1876 a Red Shirt force in Hamburg, South Carolina — a nearly all-Black town governed by Black officials — used a manufactured road dispute as a pretext to besiege the Black militia in their armory, shell it with a cannon brought from Georgia, and after the militiamen surrendered, execute several of them by name in the dark.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The massacre was explicitly the opening move of a deliberate campaign, not a spontaneous riot: it followed the Mississippi Plan's written playbook of manufacturing a pretext, escalating to violence, and using the terror to suppress Republican turnout for months. Hamburg sat just across the Savannah River from Georgia, and the attackers brought artillery from across state lines, showing the degree of advance planning involved.

events.label: Red Shirts campaign in South Carolina
